title: The AI incident disclosure shadow: tracking AI incidents into U.S. securities filings
new_audit_note: - **chincholikar-incident-disclosure** — [Frontiers publisher abstract](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1969275/abstract) read. The authors match 307 reported incidents to 21 US issuers and identify incident-specific disclosures in four cases within the specified SEC-filing universe. They emphasize dependence on incident recording and issuer matching; this does not assess legal compliance or all investor communications. Methods and full article not read in this pass.
prior_status_reported: FULL TEXT read (HTML) 2026-11-02 — abstract through conclusion with tables; references truncated. Title as published: 'The AI incident disclosure shadow: tracking AI incidents into U.S. securities filings'. DESIGN: pre-registered; 1,389 AI Incident Database incidents (2019-2026) linked to U.S.-listed issuers → 307 matched incidents across 21 issuers (Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, Microsoft dominate); filing universe = Forms 8-K/10-K/10-Q within 12 months of each incident (6/18/24-month windows tested in robustness); four-tier coding (T1 incident-specific, T2 legal-consequence only, T3 generic same-family language, T4 none); blind second coding; issuer-clustered bootstrap; retrieval audits. FINDINGS (exact): 'Only 4 incidents (1.3%; 95% CI 0.4-3.3) received incident-specific disclosure, and 7 (2.3%; 0.9-4.6) received any substantive disclosure'; 'The remaining 300 incidents (97.7%; 95.4-99.1) form an AI incident disclosure shadow'; 278 T3 incidents but only 84 matched both technology and harm families — '70.4% (64.9-75.4) of incidents had at most weakly related filing language'; substantive cases clustered on financial/legal channels (Zillow ~$304M write-down; GM Cruise '$478 million Cruise restructuring adjustment'); no detectable severity gradient (p = 0.61, power 23.3%); shadow rate 92.5-99.0% across robustness specs. LIMITS: AIID is media-derived — 'a conditional denominator... not population rates for all corporate AI incidents'; filing universe limited (non-repetition in filings != unavailability to investors); issuer attribution judgment; T2 lacks demonstrated inter-coder reliability (T1+T2 an upper bound); 'descriptive, not a legal-materiality or compliance determination'.

Bill text (§§16000.4/16100.4 Bus. & Prof. Code): before initial licensing the operator must 'provide its water supplier, under penalty of perjury, an estimate of the expected water use'; annual-use self-certification at renewal; covered facilities = IT load >10 kW and 20 W/sq ft of conditioned floor area; the text does NOT itemise end uses — the toolkit's 'loophole to exclude' cooling/construction water overstates a silence in the text. title: Cloud services market investigation — final decision (adverse effects on competition; SMS recommendation)
new_audit_note: - **cma-cloud-services-mi** — [UK CMA case page](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/cloud-services-market-investigation). Read: case description and final-report outcome summary. The CMA investigated supply of public cloud infrastructure in the UK and recommended prioritising strategic-market-status investigations of the two largest providers. The final decision and appendices were not reread in this pass, and UK conclusions should not be treated as Southeast Asian market measurements.
prior_status_reported: FULL TEXT read (summary of final decision, 8 pp, 2 Nov 2026) — the complete 8-page summary; the 637-page final decision report and appendices (incl. Appendix D market structure and Appendix R market power) UNREAD; case page read for timeline. FINDINGS (official, page-anchored): definition — cloud services give 'customers access to shared computing resources on demand so that the customers do not need to own the underlying hardware and software' (IaaS + PaaS) (para 2); UK customer spend £10.5bn in 2024, growing ~30%/yr since 2020; 'Cloud services also underpin AI model development and deployment' (para 3). Concentration: IaaS 'highly concentrated' — Microsoft and AWS each [30-40]% share of supply 2024 (UK+EEA scope), Google [5-10]%; PaaS Microsoft [20-30]%, AWS [10-20]% (para 5-6); concentration 'likely to endure' (para 7); both leaders earn returns 'substantially above their cost of capital' (para 8). Vertical integration: 'Microsoft, AWS and Google are all strong vertically integrated providers of accelerated compute and AI-related cloud services, including through partnerships with AI model developers. Other cloud providers are significantly weaker in this respect' (para 12); AI 'yet to materially alter the competitive dynamics in cloud services' (para 13). Barriers: entry needs 'significant capital investment in fixed assets such as data centres, networks and servers... largely a sunk cost' (para 17) + economies of scale + broad portfolios. Switching: 'less than 1% of customers switch provider each year' (para 24); 'A key commercial barrier is the presence and magnitude of egress fees' (para 26); technical barriers from differentiated features/interfaces (para 27); committed spend agreements widespread but not currently judged harmful (para 28). Microsoft licensing: its practices 'are adversely impacting the competitiveness of AWS and Google' and 'reducing competition in cloud services markets' (paras 35-36c; relevant products: Windows Server, SQL Server, Windows 10/11, Visual Studio, productivity suites — fn 2). DECISION: adverse effects on competition (AECs) from (a) concentration+barriers → 'significant unilateral market power', (b) switching/multi-cloud lock-in, (c) Microsoft's licensing practices (para 36); illustration: prices 5% above well-functioning markets ≈ £500m/yr extra cost to UK customers (fn 3). REMEDY: recommend the CMA Board prioritise SMS investigations to consider designating Microsoft and AWS with strategic market status under the DMCC Act (paras 38-42); options expected before the Board in early 2026. LIMITS: UK+EEA geographic scope only; shares published as bracketed ranges; not a global or Southeast Asia finding; the SMS designation is a recommendation, not yet a decision; the unverified 'voluntary commitments accepted' narrative circulating in secondary reporting is NOT on the official case page and is not used here. | TECHNICAL DEEPENING (Addendum 33, 2 Nov 2026): the final decision report's egress/switching analysis READ at paras 6.341-6.417 (PDF pp. 330-349); appendices L-Q (egress background, cost scenarios, free switching, customer views, internal documents, provider costs) located but NOT read. GEOGRAPHY AND DATE CHECKED: market scope 'UK+EEA' (fn 1); CMA's switching-cost scenario built on 'UK customer-level data on the mean volumes of data they stored for each year from 2018 to 2022' (para 6.406a, from AWS/Microsoft/Google information requests); list prices from provider websites 'for the applicable UK region' — 'London' region for Google and AWS — accessed 29 Jan 2024 (fn 1679-1680); provider egress-payment shares reported for 2023 (paras 6.349-6.352); free switching programmes introduced 2024 considered (para 6.344d). METHOD: one-off full-data-transfer scenario, cost expressed as % of annual spend spread over a typical three-year contract (para 6.406); provider-submitted alternatives (AWS customer-level analysis, Appendix M) given less weight because analyses based on customers who actually switched 'will tend to exclude any customers that found egress fees too high and were deterred from switching' (para 6.404) — a selection-bias critique. RESULTS (percentages REDACTED as [x-y] ranges in the public version): [0-5]% to [5-10]% of customers would pay egress fees above [5-10]% of annual spend per year over a three-year contract; the smallest customers (£1,000-£10,000/yr band) face the highest proportional fees; up-front (unspread): [10-20]% to [20-30]% of customers would face >[5-10]% of annual spend (paras 6.407-6.410). INTERPRETATION CAVEATS (paras 6.411-6.412): the analysis 'is likely to understate the effect of egress fees on switching' because total cloud spend includes non-data-intensive workloads; list prices ignore discounts (incl. CSA discounts, common among the largest customers) and premium alternatives (eg direct connect); 'the combined effect of these different factors is ambiguous'. CONCLUSION FOR THIS PROJECT: the switching/egress findings rest on UK-specific customer data (2018-2022 storage volumes; Jan 2024 list prices; 2023 payment shares) — they are a UK+EEA regulator's measured analysis, NOT Southeast Asian or global figures, and the exact percentages are confidential in the public version.
